newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Peters threat to quit debate after changes made.
newsitem.headline: Peters threat to quit debate after changes made.

text.p: New Zealand First leader Winston Peters last night threatened to quit the next Holmes leaders debate on Television One after claiming that political pressure had been used to change the programme's format, the New Zealand Press Association reported on Wednesday.
"I've got a simple message for TVNZ and it is this: you're gutless," Peters said at a public meeting in Dannevirke.

The comments followed news that TVNZ was to change the speaking order and seating arrangement at next Monday's debate, and that it plans to add the leaders of the United, Act and Christian Coalition parties to the debate.
Staff from Prime Minister Jim Bolger's office had protested over the format of the first Holmes debate last week, claiming other party leaders had a fairer deal than Mr Bolger.
Bolger in particular protested over the use of the "worm", a device in which a studio panel of undecided voters rated each leader's performance.
Peters said TVNZ had not kept an agreement to consult the other leaders before changing the format.
Bolger had performed in an "appalling" fashion in last week's debate.
"I know that Jim Bolger was furious with his performance... I heard it myself through the dressing room wall. It was everyone's fault except his.
"So what did National threaten TVNZ with, for TVNZ to so cravenly capitulate? Was it Mr Bolger's withdrawal from the second debate? So what? Up would have gone the IQ level and the debating level.
"Was it threatening to sell TVNZ should National be re-elected? Or was it direct pressure from the party political appointments on the TVNZ board?"
Peters then named TVNZ chairman Norman Geary as a National party fundraiser.
Peters said, like Bolger, he had not known before the debate if a worm had been used and he did not care.
Bolger could not hack the pace and needed cheerleaders and "political pygmies" the Christian Coalition, United and Act to help him.
Peters said the first he had learned of the changes was on watching One Network News. TVNZ had failed to honour an agreement to consult other party leaders before changing the show's format.
"The involvement of New Zealand First is now in grave doubt," he said.
The party had put up for long enough with not being covered by TVNZ when other political parties were being covered, he said.
"It is now quite plain that TVNZ are so graceless that they buckle to Prime Ministerial pressure 10 days out from an election and don't have the decency to even inform us."
Peters said the changes were an example of "political bias" on the part of TVNZ, but he was prepared to take on and beat corporates, the media and all other political parties.
"Nothing, and I mean nothing, is going to prevent New Zealand First taking its message direct to the New Zealand people."
Peters, travelling with media and party officials on his campaign bus, this morning continued a tour of the North Island's East Coast with stops at Waipukurau and Hastings.
